summary: Defines M2PA, a protocol that carries SS7 Message Transfer Part Level 3 signaling over IP using SCTP. It is used between SS7 signaling points and may also run alongside standard SS7 links. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone networks send control messages over special lines. This memo lets those messages travel over the internet instead, like using a delivery truck rather than a private road.

questions: how does ss7 run over ip
subtitle: Lets two SS7 signaling nodes keep their MTP3 layer and swap the old serial link for an SCTP association over IP.

tldr.problem: Telephone signaling nodes speak SS7, and carrying that signaling over an IP network would let them reach IP-side databases and applications and could cut operating costs. They need a way to do it while MTP3 keeps working exactly as before.
tldr.mechanism: M2PA sits between MTP3 and SCTP and replaces MTP2. It gives MTP3 the same interface MTP2 does, treats each SCTP association as one SS7 link, and uses two message types, User Data and Link Status, on two SCTP streams.
tldr.outcome: IP Signaling Points can act as ordinary SS7 nodes with their own point codes, including as signaling gateways to the traditional network. It is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 4165 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2005, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on SCTP (RFC 2960) and the signaling transport framework in RFC 2719.

sections.title: Why SS7 Needs an IP Adaptation
sections.content:
RFC 4165 defines the MTP2 User Peer-to-Peer Adaptation Layer (M2PA). It transports Signaling System Number 7 (SS7) Message Transfer Part Level 3 (MTP3) messages over IP, using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) as the transport.

The motivation is convergence. SS7 nodes would gain access to databases and other devices in the IP domain that do not use SS7 links, IP telephony applications would gain access to SS7 services, and there may be cost and performance advantages when traditional signaling links are replaced by IP connections.

An SS7 node with an IP connection is called an IP Signaling Point (IPSP). The RFC wants IPSPs to work as traditional SS7 nodes, with full MTP3 message handling and network management, but using the IP network instead of SS7 links.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone networks have their own private mail system for control notes. This memo lets them use the internet's mail system instead, and the phone gear still behaves as if nothing changed.

sections.title: Where M2PA Sits in the Stack
sections.content:
M2PA is an adaptation module in the signaling transport framework of RFC 2719. It gives MTP3 an interface and services similar to MTP2, so in effect MTP2 and the lower layers of the SS7 stack are replaced by an IP equivalent: M2PA over SCTP over IP. The SCTP association acts as one SS7 link between two IPSPs.

In a Signaling Gateway (SG), the node has a traditional SS7 link on one side (MTP2 over MTP1) and an M2PA/SCTP/IP connection on the other. The SG acts as a Signal Transfer Point. Every IPSP must have its own SS7 point code.

The RFC contrasts M2PA with the MTP2 User Adaptation Layer (M2UA), which backhauls MTP3/MTP2 primitives to a remote entity. With M2PA the IPSP processes the primitives itself, the SG-to-IPSP connection is an SS7 link, and the SG is an SS7 node with a point code and can host upper layers such as SCCP. With M2UA the SG has no point code and no MTP3.
sections.plainLanguage: M2PA is a translator sitting between the phone system's brain and the internet delivery service. The brain talks to it exactly as it used to talk to the old cable.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
All fields are sent in network byte order. Every message starts with a Common Message Header of Version, Spare, Message Class and Message Type, followed by a Message Length that counts the whole message including the header. Version is 1 and the only valid Message Class is 11.

Next comes the M2PA-specific header, which holds a Backward Sequence Number (BSN) and a Forward Sequence Number (FSN), each in a 24-bit field with an unused octet in front. The BSN is the FSN of the last message received from the peer. Both range from 0 to 16,777,215.

There are two message types. User Data (type 1) carries the priority octet, SIO and SIF from an MTP3 message signal unit. It must not carry the flag, sequence numbers, indicator bits, length indicator or check bits of MTP2. Link Status (type 2) carries a state value, for example Alignment, Ready, Processor Outage or Busy, and performs the role of MTP2 link status signal units.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a label on the outside with its type and size, plus two counters like page numbers so each side can tell which pages the other has received. Inside is either real mail or a short status note.

sections.title: Streams, Acknowledgements and Priorities
sections.content:
M2PA does not copy everything from MTP2. SCTP already gives reliable, ordered delivery and a checksum, so M2PA needs no flags, zero-bit insertion, checksum, error rate monitor or retransmissions. M2PA still keeps sent User Data messages in a retransmit queue until they are acknowledged, because MTP3 may need them for a changeover.

MTP2 sends fill-in signal units continuously, but M2PA has no equivalent because an IP network is shared. Acknowledgements ride on the next User Data message. If there is nothing to send, M2PA SHOULD send an empty User Data message without delay, and that message does not increment the FSN.

Each association has two streams in each direction. Stream 0 carries Link Status messages such as Alignment, Proving, Busy and Out of Service. Stream 1 carries User Data plus the Link Status messages that must stay in order with data (Processor Outage, Processor Recovered, and Ready at the end of an outage). This lets Link Status traffic take priority, as it does in MTP2, and M2PA SHOULD read the Link Status stream first.

Each link maps to one SCTP association, identified by the IP addresses and ports of both ends, and each association maps to a Signaling Link Code. At least one end SHOULD use the registered M2PA port.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two lanes on the road: a fast lane for short status notes and a normal lane for the real mail. Receipts are tucked into the next letter, or sent as an empty envelope if there is no letter.

sections.title: Link Alignment, Outages and Changeover
sections.content:
After the SCTP association comes up, M2PA sends Link Status Out of Service, then Alignment to begin link alignment. Proving messages follow, sent at a Proving_Interval, and the proving period can be omitted if the applicable MTP2 standard allows. Link Status Ready confirms both ends are done, after which MTP3 MAY send data. The messages replace the MTP2 SIOS, SIO, SIN, SIE and FISU units, and the usual MTP2 timers such as T1, T2, T3 and T4 apply.

In a processor outage, M2PA sends Link Status Processor Outage. A node in local outage MUST buffer and not acknowledge incoming User Data. When it recovers it sends Processor Recovered, and the two ends exchange Link Status Ready messages whose BSN lets them resynchronize sequence numbers.

For flow control, Busy and Busy Ended replace MTP2's SIB signal. The receiving peer starts timer T6 and stops T7, and MUST NOT send User Data while the other end is busy.

For changeover, M2PA retrieves unacknowledged and unsent User Data for MTP3 so traffic moves to another link without loss. Because M2PA sequence numbers are 24 bits while MTP2's are seven bits, MTP3 MUST use the Extended Changeover Order and Acknowledgement messages. M2PA also notes that SCTP slow start can delay messages during alignment and changeover.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two phones lines start talking they shake hands and test the connection. If one side needs a breather it says so, and both sides then agree where they left off before carrying on.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The security section is short. M2PA carries telephony signaling, so it MUST address the needs of end users, network providers and the applications involved, and local regulation may add requirements. Implementers MUST follow the guidelines in RFC 3788.

IANA assigned port 3565 for M2PA over SCTP and also for TCP in case an M2PA-over-TCP specification is ever written. The SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier is 5. New message classes, types and parameters are assigned by IETF Consensus under RFC 2434, and this document registers class 11 and message types 1 and 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Because these messages run phone calls, they need to be kept safe, and the memo points to another document for how. It also reserves an official mailbox number so everyone knows where to deliver M2PA messages.
